name: H1-summary
output: The narrative begins with the Huns, described as a vast Tartar horde, bursting into lands north of the Euxine around A.D. 372 [PDF p. 61]. They nearly exterminated the Alans before crushing the Ostrogoths, who were forced into vassalage or fled south [PDF p. 61]. The Visigoths, viewing slavery to such savages as intolerable, requested permission from the Emperor to cross the Danube [PDF p. 62]. At this time, the Empire was divided; Valens ruled the East, characterized by the author as stupid, cowardly, and avaricious, while Valentinian held the West [PDF p. 62]. Valens, though dismayed, allowed the Goths to settle as subject-allies if they surrendered arms and hostages [PDF p. 63]. However, Roman officials accepted bribes to let Goths retain weapons, and Governor Lupicinus extorted food supplies, driving Goths to desperation [PDF p. 63]. A chance affray at Marcianopolis, where Lupicinus recklessly ordered the murder of Gothic guests, ignited a full-scale war [PDF p. 64]. The conflict initially resembled third-century raids, with Goths sacking towns and joined by runaway slaves [PDF p. 64]. In 378, Valens personally led a 60,000-man army against the Goths, who had adopted cavalry tactics [PDF p. 65]. At Adrianople, Gothic cavalry overwhelmed the Roman flank, causing a chaotic collapse where packed Roman units were cut down [PDF p. 66]. The battle resulted in 40,000 Roman deaths and the loss of high-ranking commanders, marking the worst defeat since Cannae [PDF p. 67]. The army was never reorganized on old lines [PDF p. 67]. The victorious Goths approached Constantinople but, daunted by its vast walls, abandoned siege machines and retreated to Thrace [PDF p. 67].
